newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Brcko is Bosnia's burning post-election issue.
newsitem.headline: Brcko is Bosnia's burning post-election issue.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Bosnian refugees and displaced people on Friday began travelling to their old homes to vote in Saturday's post-war election in a colossal movement of populations.

Thousands of Serb refugees from neighbouring Yugoslavia began moving late in the evening, creating what are expected to be major traffic jams across the dangerously narrow, potholed roads of northern Bosnia.
Those hoping to vote in the Serbs' north-western territories will have to pass through the town of Brcko, the most coveted piece of real estate in the 43-month-long war.
To Serbs, Brcko is the key to the so-called Posavina Corridor which links Bosnian Serb territories in the east and west along the river Sava -- the border with Croatia.
To Moslems and Croats, the town is the gateway through hostile Serb territory to vital markets in Croatia and eastern Europe beyond.
During the war, Moslems concentrated their forces on Brcko, and managed to squeeze the bottleneck to a mere three km (two miles), threatening to cleave the Serb territories in two.

Before war errupted in 1992, the town was mainly Moslem and Croat. The issue of who should control Brcko was so sensitive that the architects of the Dayton peace accord chose to leave its status to international arbitration.
All the Bosnian Serb parties kept the issue of Brcko high in their election campaigns.

Bosnian Serb parliamentary speaker Momcilo Krajisnik, running for the future Bosnian three-man multi-ethnic presidency, called it the "alpha and omega of the Serb people" -- a biblical reference that implied the town is at the very heart of Serb survival.
The Serbs claim Dayton gave them control over Brcko, but have so far stalled the work of the arbitration commission.

Senior Bosnian Serb sources told Reuters there was genuine pressure from the West to put the town under five years of international administration. "This violates the Dayton peace accord and is a bitter blow to the peace effort," one said.

Apart from gaining access to the Sava River, the mainly Moslem Bosnian government also wants thousands of refugees to be allowed to return to their homes in Brcko -- a right guaranteed in the Dayton documents.

Nationalists on all three sides have prevented refugees from crossing the so-called inter-entity boundary line (IEBL) intended as a purely porous administrative division between the Bosnian Serb republic and the Moslem-Croat federation.
In reality, the IEBL has been transformed into a closely guarded and sealed border for members of rival ethnic groups.
Over the past nine months, scores of those who wanted to exercise their rights have been attacked, and some even killed.

But on Saturday, they will have an opportunity to vote in their former homes under the watchful eyes of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and its muscles -- 60,000 heavily-armed peace troops.
Bosnian Serb media have been calling for calm, admonishing thoughts of violence. "Remember, security at polling stations is inviolate," local Serb radio told its listeners in Brcko.
To calm tempers, alcohol sales have been banned until after the elections.

Despite the desire to visit their homes and the appeals for calm, Moslems are not expected to risk the trip to Brcko in vast numbers. OSCE representatives believe that no more than 1,000 will make the journey.
But those that do will be able to choose to vote in the centre of town or at an alternative polling station three km (two miles) further west and close to an American checkpoint -- just in case.
